---
title: "What Makes a Problem RL"
---

Most of us met reinforcement learning as a separate subject. It arrived with its own vocabulary
(agents, environments, MDPs, Bellman equations, Q-tables, exploration) and its own canonical
examples (gridworlds, Atari, Go), and it was easy to come away believing that RL is a different
*kind* of machine learning, with different models and different losses. Then language-model
post-training started calling things RL that look, from the outside, like fine-tuning a
transformer with a slightly unusual loss. Both impressions are half right. This chapter makes
the boundary precise. The claim it defends is the first thesis of the book: **RL is defined by
where the training data comes from and what kind of feedback it carries, not by the model or
the loss.** Once that is clear, the rest of the classical apparatus (returns, values, the Bellman
equation, the split between value-based and policy-based methods) can be introduced as answers
to specific problems that this kind of feedback creates, rather than as a separate world.

## Three kinds of feedback

Take one model and put it in three situations.

**A classifier.** An image comes in, the model outputs a distribution over labels, and a
dataset tells it the correct label. Training pushes up the log-probability of that label. Note
two things about the signal. It says *what the right answer was*, regardless of what the model
predicted. And the images arrive from a fixed dataset that has nothing to do with the model's
current behavior.

**A recommender that shows one item.** A user arrives, the model picks one article to show, and
the system observes whether the user clicked. Now the signal is different in kind. A click on
article 3 says that article 3 was good enough to click. It says nothing about articles 1, 2 or 4,
which were never shown. And which article got shown, and therefore which piece of feedback
exists at all, was decided by the model itself. This is the setting Li et al. formalized as a
*contextual bandit* for news recommendation [@li2010contextual].

**A game.** The model makes a move, then another, then forty more, and at the end it learns
whether it won. Now there is a third difficulty: the outcome cannot be traced to any single
move. Some early move might have lost the game; the final move might have been brilliant. The
feedback is *delayed*, and credit has to be spread across the sequence somehow.

Sutton and Barto put the first distinction at the center of their textbook: "the most important
feature distinguishing reinforcement learning from other types of learning is that it uses
training information that evaluates the actions taken rather than instructs by giving correct
actions" [@sutton2018reinforcement, ch. 2]. *Instructive* feedback, they write, "indicates the
correct action to take, independently of the action actually taken"; *evaluative* feedback
"indicates how good the action taken was, but not whether it was the best or the worst action
possible". Their opening chapter names the second and third distinctions as well:
"trial-and-error search and delayed reward" are "the two most important distinguishing features
of reinforcement learning" [@sutton2018reinforcement, sec. 1.1]. The three situations above are
those three properties, switched on one at a time.

1. **Instructive vs. evaluative feedback.** A label says what the right answer was. A reward
   says only how good the answer you gave was, and nothing about the answers you did not give.
2. **Fixed vs. self-generated data.** In supervised learning the data distribution is given. In
   RL the learner's own policy decides which data it sees, so the training distribution moves as
   the learner changes.
3. **Immediate vs. delayed consequences.** Either a reward can be traced to the action that
   caused it, or credit must be spread across a sequence of actions.

Placing the familiar problem types in this space gives the following table.

| | Feedback | Data | Consequences |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised learning | instructive | fixed | immediate |
| Contextual bandit | evaluative | self-generated | immediate |
| Full RL (MDP) | evaluative | self-generated | delayed |
| Imitation learning / SFT | instructive | fixed (the expert's distribution, not the learner's) | delayed at test time |

The contextual bandit sits exactly between supervised learning and full RL. Sutton and Barto
call it *associative search* and describe it the same way: like full RL "in that [it involves]
learning a policy", but like a bandit "in that each action affects only the immediate reward. If
actions are allowed to affect the next situation as well as the reward, then we have the full
reinforcement learning problem" [@sutton2018reinforcement, sec. 2.9].

The last row deserves a second look, because it is where language-model training starts.
Imitation learning, and its LLM incarnation supervised fine-tuning (SFT), trains on instructive
feedback from a fixed dataset of an expert's behavior. During training it looks exactly like
supervised learning. At test time, however, the learner acts in a sequence, and its own earlier
actions decide which situations it ends up in. If it makes a mistake it reaches states the
expert never visited, where it was never trained, and errors compound. Ross and Bagnell made
this quantitative: a policy that errs with probability $\epsilon$ on the expert's state
distribution can incur a cost that grows as $T^2\epsilon$ over a horizon of $T$ steps, rather
than $T\epsilon$, and the bound is tight [@ross2010efficient; @ross2011reduction]. In sequence
generation the same mismatch has a name of its own, *exposure bias*: Ranzato et al. used it for
"a model [that] is only exposed to the training data distribution, instead of its own
predictions" [@ranzato2016sequence]. Their remedy, notably, was to train the text generator on
its own samples with REINFORCE, years before RLHF. The general remedy for training on someone
else's distribution is to train on your own, which is the second property in the list above.

So the "RL is a different category" intuition is half true. As the rest of this chapter shows,
the mathematics is mostly shared. What really differs is the data-generating process.

## One model, one gradient, three signals

The claim that only the signal differs can be tested directly. The book's experiments run on a
small *enumerable language* ([described in the testbed appendix](../appendix-testbed.qmd)): five
tokens, responses of exactly four tokens, so $5^4 = 625$ possible responses, and four prompts.
A reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ was fit by maximum likelihood to a synthetic corpus, and a
response is *correct* if its tokens sum to the prompt's target modulo 5, a toy version of a
verifiable math answer. Because there are only 625 responses, the probability that the current
policy answers correctly can be computed exactly at every step rather than estimated.

Starting from $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, the same policy is trained three ways, with the same optimizer
and learning rate, and with the same final operation: a gradient step on
$\sum_i w_i \log\pi_\theta(y_i\mid x_i)$ over a batch of responses $y_i$. Only the responses and
the weights differ.

- **Instructive:** the batch is demonstrations, correct answers drawn from an expert (here,
  $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ restricted to correct responses), each with weight 1. This is supervised
  learning, or SFT.
- **Evaluative, self-generated:** the batch is the policy's own samples, weighted by their reward
  minus the average reward of the other samples for the same prompt. This is REINFORCE, the
  basic policy-gradient algorithm the [next chapter](02-policy-gradients.qmd) derives.
- **Evaluative, fixed log:** the batch is samples that $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ generated (a log of
  someone else's behavior), weighted by their reward. Responses that happened to be correct get
  pushed up; nothing else does.

![Three training runs of the same policy, differing only in the feedback signal. Left and middle: exact probability of a correct answer for the hardest prompt ($\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is right 2% of the time) and the easiest (71%), median and range over 5 seeds; 8 samples per prompt per step, the x-axis counts samples over all four prompts. Right: on the hard prompt, the share of each batch that was a correct answer. Demonstrations are informative from the first step. The learner's own samples carry almost no signal while it rarely answers correctly, then the signal grows as it improves, because its policy chooses its data. A fixed log never improves, so learning from it stays slow.](../images/three_kinds_of_feedback.png){#fig-three-kinds-of-feedback}

@fig-three-kinds-of-feedback shows the three runs. On the easy prompt all three behave almost
identically: when most answers are already right, it hardly matters whether the signal says "this
is correct" or "this one scored 1". The hard prompt separates them, and each difference traces
back to one of the properties in the table.

Demonstrations are informative from the first step, because instructive feedback does not
depend on what the learner currently does. The learner's own samples carry almost no signal at
first: with a 2% hit rate, most groups of eight answers contain no correct answer at all, every
reward is zero, and the gradient is zero. Evaluative feedback cannot tell the learner what it
should have said. Once a few correct answers have been reinforced, the policy produces more of
them, its batches become informative, and learning accelerates sharply (the right panel). That
acceleration is the self-generated property at work. The fixed log has the same evaluative
signal but no such feedback loop: the share of useful samples stays at $\pi_{\text{ref}}$'s 2%
forever, and after the same number of samples the policy is still right only about 36% of the
time.

The figure also shows something the table did not predict. On the hard prompt, RL overtakes
supervised learning. The two runs are not chasing the same thing. The expert's demonstrations
spread probability over all the correct answers, and SFT has to reproduce that whole spread: at
the end, the SFT policy still puts more than 1% probability on each of 19 different responses,
with an entropy of about 3.6 nats, essentially the expert's. The REINFORCE policy is rewarded
only for being correct, so it is free to pile its mass onto whichever correct answer it found
first; it ends with about 0.1 nats of entropy and one dominant response. Maximizing expected
reward rewards collapse onto one good answer; imitation rewards reproducing a distribution. That
contrast returns with a precise form, forward versus reverse KL, in the
[chapter on keeping updates stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd), and in the debate about what
RL does to a model's diversity in the [synthesis chapter](11-what-rl-does-to-a-model.qmd).

::: {.callout-important title="Classical lineage — this is the exploration problem"}
The hard prompt's slow start is the exploration problem from bandit theory: an agent that only
learns from the outcomes of its own actions cannot learn about actions it never tries. In
classical RL the fix is deliberate exploration (ε-greedy, optimism, Thompson sampling). In LLM
post-training it is mostly sampling from a pretrained policy that already gets *some* answers
right, which is why the starting policy matters so much.
:::

## MDPs, returns, values and the Bellman equation, compactly

The third property, delayed consequences, is what the full RL formalism exists to handle. This
section collects only what the rest of the book needs; the
[RL chapter of modern-ai-systems-and-methods](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/modern-ai-systems-and-methods/chapters/10-reinforcement-learning-bandits.html)
and Sutton and Barto give the full treatment.

A **Markov decision process** has states $s$, actions $a$, a transition distribution
$P(s'\mid s,a)$, a reward, and a discount factor $\gamma$. A **policy** $\pi(a\mid s)$ is a
distribution over actions in each state. It exists because the agent has to act somewhere, and a
distribution (rather than a fixed rule) is what lets it explore and what a gradient can move.
Running a policy produces a trajectory $s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, r_2, \dots$, and the **return**
from step $t$ is the discounted sum of the rewards that follow,

$$
G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \gamma^2 r_{t+3} + \cdots .
$$

The return exists because the quantity worth maximizing is not the next reward but everything
that follows from an action. The discount makes infinite sums finite. In episodes that always
end, such as a response that stops after a finite number of tokens, $\gamma = 1$ is allowed, and
LLM post-training uses it.

The return is a random variable, and noisy. The **value** of a state averages it out:
$V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t\mid s_t = s]$, the expected return from $s$ when following $\pi$.
The **action value** conditions on the first action as well:
$Q^\pi(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t\mid s_t = s, a_t = a]$. Their difference, the **advantage**

$$
A^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s,a) - V^\pi(s),
$$

says how much better action $a$ is than what the policy does on average in $s$. It exists because
"this action led to a return of 7" means nothing until you know whether 7 is good in this state.
The advantage is the quantity a learning signal should really be built from, and most of the
[next chapter](02-policy-gradients.qmd) is about estimating it.

Values satisfy a recursive consistency condition, the **Bellman equation**:

$$
V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s),\; s'\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)}\big[\, r + \gamma V^\pi(s') \,\big].
$$

The value of a state is the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of wherever you
land next. This recursion gives two ways to estimate $V^\pi(s_t)$ from experience. **Monte
Carlo** estimation waits until the episode ends and uses the observed return $G_t$ as the
target. It is unbiased, but it has high variance, because $G_t$ accumulates the randomness of
every later action and transition. **Temporal-difference** (TD) learning uses the one-step
target $r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1})$ instead, plugging in the *current estimate* of the next
state's value. This is **bootstrapping**: it has much lower variance, because only one step of
randomness enters, but it is biased whenever the estimate $V$ is wrong, which early in training
it always is. Multi-step and $\lambda$-weighted targets interpolate between the two. Bootstrapping
also carries a known hazard: Sutton and Barto's *deadly triad* is the combination of function
approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training, any two of which are manageable but all
three of which risk "instability and divergence" [@sutton2018reinforcement, sec. 11.3]. Keep
this trade-off in mind. Variance versus bias is the axis along which every advantage estimator
in this book (Monte Carlo returns, learned critics, GAE, leave-one-out baselines, group
normalization) is placed.

## Two ways to get a policy

There are two broad ways to turn this apparatus into an agent.

**Value-based** methods learn $Q$ and derive the policy from it, usually by acting greedily:
$\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s,a)$. Q-learning and DQN are the canonical examples. They are
off-policy by construction (they can learn about the greedy policy while behaving otherwise),
they reuse experience efficiently through bootstrapping and replay, and they dominate domains
with small discrete action sets and dense rewards.

**Policy-based** methods parameterize the policy directly, $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, and adjust
$\theta$ by gradient ascent on expected return. Sutton and Barto list what this buys
[@sutton2018reinforcement, sec. 13.1]: a softmax policy over action preferences "can approach a
deterministic policy", whereas ε-greedy action selection over values always keeps an ε chance of
a random action; it can represent stochastic policies with arbitrary probabilities; and the
policy can be parameterized "in any way, as long as" it is differentiable, for example by "a
deep artificial neural network".

Language models went policy-based, and the reasons follow from the setting rather than from
fashion. Each of the following is developed later, in the
[chapter on the LLM as a policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd).

- **The action space is huge.** At the token level it is the vocabulary, tens of thousands of
  actions in every state. At the response level, the natural level for a reward, it is the set of
  all sequences, astronomically large. An $\arg\max$ over $Q$ at the response level is not
  computable, and token-level $Q$-learning would have to bootstrap through long sequences.
- **A good parametric policy already exists.** Pretraining produces a strong
  $\pi_\theta(y_t\mid x, y_{<t})$, a softmax over the next token. A policy-based method starts
  from it; a value-based method would have to learn a $Q$ function from scratch, or find a way to
  read one out of the language model.
- **The reward usually arrives once, at the end.** With a single sequence-level reward the
  problem behaves much like a contextual bandit over whole responses, where the machinery of
  bootstrapping has little to work with.
- **The policy must stay close to a reference distribution.** Post-training is supposed to
  adjust a pretrained model, not replace it. A KL penalty to the starting policy is natural
  when the policy is the object being optimized, and awkward when it is implicit in a $Q$ function.

Value-based ideas did not disappear. They returned in narrower roles: the learned **critic**
$V_\phi$ that PPO-based RLHF trains as a baseline (an estimate of $V^\pi$, not a policy); process
reward models, which score partial solutions and play a role close to a value estimate
([the rewards chapter](05-rewards.qmd)); value functions trained to *guide decoding* from a frozen
model [@mudgal2024controlled]; and offline $Q$-learning for language generation
[@snell2022offline]. The dominant recipes for post-training, however, are policy gradients, and
the more recent ones have even dropped the critic.

::: {.callout-important title="Classical lineage — this is the policy-gradient branch of RL"}
Everything from REINFORCE to PPO, GRPO and on-policy distillation belongs to the policy-based
branch: parameterize $\pi_\theta$ directly and follow the gradient of expected reward. The
value-based branch (Q-learning, DQN) survives in LLM work mainly as critics, value-like reward
models and value-guided decoding.
:::

## LLM post-training touches every corner of this table

Return to the three properties. A language model generating a response, scored by a reward at
the end, receives evaluative feedback, on data it generated itself, with consequences that
arrive only after a whole sequence of token choices. That is the full RL row of the table. The
same model trained by SFT on demonstrations is the imitation-learning row, with the
compounding-error weakness that comes with it. Train it on a fixed dataset of someone else's
responses with rewards attached and it is offline RL. Treat the whole response as a single action
with a single reward and it is a contextual bandit, which, as the
[chapter on the LLM as a policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) argues, is often the most useful
way to see it.

Every method in this book can be located by asking the three questions of this chapter: what
does the feedback say, who generated the data, and how far is the reward from the actions that
earned it? The [next chapter](02-policy-gradients.qmd) shows that once those questions are
answered, what remains is a single gradient formula with two dials.

## Connections

- [Policy Gradients](02-policy-gradients.qmd) turns the experiment in this chapter into algebra:
  the supervised gradient and the REINFORCE gradient are the same operation, pushing up
  $\log\pi_\theta$ of some responses, differing only in which responses and with what weight.
- [The LLM as a Policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) makes the mapping from MDP to text
  generation formal (state, action, transition, reward, episode) and explains which parts of
  this chapter's classical machinery survive in LLM post-training and which do not.
- [Keeping Updates Stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) explains the collapse seen in
  @fig-three-kinds-of-feedback: maximizing reward is mode-seeking, imitation is mass-covering,
  and the direction of a KL divergence is the precise statement of the difference.
- [Learning by Imitating a Better Distribution](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd) returns
  to the "fixed log" run: training on filtered or reward-weighted samples is a whole family of
  methods, and this chapter's experiment shows both why it is robust and why it is slow.
